name: Adamia
lede: Adamia is a dark, muted purple from the Maerz and Paul dictionary, so close to a handful of other library purples that they are nearly indistinguishable on screen.

sections.title: A name in the library
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary first records Adamia in 1928, on plate 45, swatch L 11 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system classes it as a dark purple, about 3.3 units from that block's center [1]. Who or what the name honors is not stated in the sources consulted [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[light-aubergine]], [[imperial]], [[toga]] and [[japanese-violet]], at 3.6, 3.6, 3.9 and 4.3 ΔE [1]. All four share Adamia's low lightness and muted purple chroma; a reader would struggle to tell them apart without the labels [2]. Munsell notation places Adamia at 5.9P 2.4/6.3 [1]. The hex value, #4E2C57, is a screen approximation of the dictionary plate, not a measured pigment [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this purple in only 2 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a rate under one in ten thousand [3]. Both are a dark-purple accent rather than a dominant color: a mid-1800s royal portrait, Nicaise de Keyser's *Portrait of Grand Princess Anna Pavlovna* (1850), and Alfred Sisley's *The forge in Marly-le-Roi* (1875) [3]. The matches lean toward Belgian and French paintings, but the count is too small to generalize [3]. These are computed color matches on varnished, photographed canvases, not pigment identifications [3].
